name: contamination_vs_saturation
prompt: I'm running a 40-model bank (evals/fixtures/model_bank_40.csv) and I see two anomalous items. it_sat passes 100% of the time — every model passes it. it_noise passes about 45% of the time but the pattern looks random: some of my weakest models pass it and some of my strongest fail it. My colleague says both are just outliers to trim. But I think these are two different problems. How do I tell the difference between saturation and contamination statistically, and does the fix differ?
response:
Your colleague is wrong to lump them — they fail for opposite reasons, and that difference dictates whether you trim or investigate.

## The diagnostic split

| | it_sat (p = 1.0) | it_noise (p ≈ 0.45) |
|---|---|---|
| CTT difficulty | 1.0 — degenerate | 0.45 — looks informative |
| Item–rest r | undefined (zero SD) | **negative** |
| Discrimination D | 0 (trivially) | **< 0** |
| IRT read | b → −∞, a unestimable | a < 0 (inverted ICC) |
| What it means | Bank outgrew the item | Item penalizes ability |
| Fix | Safe to trim | **Investigate first** |

---

## it_sat — saturation

Everyone passes, so the item has zero variance: r_rest is undefined and test information is 0 at every θ. In IRT terms, the difficulty b sits far to the left of your whole taker distribution — every model clears it easily. The item isn't wrong; the bank has simply outgrown it. Trimming is safe. The one exception: if this item guards against a known regression (it should always pass), label it `guard` and keep it — "everyone passes" is the *goal* for a guard, not evidence of uselessness.

## it_noise — negative discrimination (not contamination)

p ≈ 0.45 is the trap. Mid-range difficulty looks maximally informative in CTT, so this item would pass a difficulty filter and fool a naive sweep. But when weaker models pass and stronger models fail, you have a **negative item–rest correlation** and a **negative D = p_top − p_bottom**. In IRT, the 2PL discrimination parameter a comes back negative — the ICC slopes downward instead of up. The item is actively penalizing ability.

This is categorically different from contamination in the 3PL sense. True contamination shows as a **high guessing parameter c**: a floor pass rate above chance even at very low θ, from models reciting memorized answers. The ICC still slopes upward — better takers still pass more. What you're describing is an inverted ICC, which 3PL can't even represent with a positive a. Your item isn't contaminated; it's broken.

**Why the fix differs:** For saturation, the item is merely stale — trim it and move on. For negative discrimination, trimming removes the symptom and hides the cause. The underlying problem — a wrong gold label, an inverted grader, a rubric that rewards failure — almost certainly affects other items you haven't flagged yet. Trimming it_noise without investigation means your other scores are also suspect at some unknown rate.

---

## How to diagnose this on your data

Run the CTT item analysis first:

```bash
python scripts/eval_item_analysis.py evals/fixtures/model_bank_40.csv \
  --taker-col taker_id --item-col item_id --score-col score
```

For it_sat you'll see p = 1.0 and a warning that r_rest is undefined (zero SD). For it_noise you'll see p ≈ 0.45 **and a `FIX` flag** because r_rest < 0 and D < 0. The script sorts fixes first, above trim candidates.

Then, since you have 40 takers (bank regime), run the IRT audit for the full picture:

```bash
python scripts/irt_eval.py evals/fixtures/model_bank_40.csv \
  --taker-col taker_id --item-col item_id --score-col score
```

it_sat will show near-zero item information across all θ, with b estimated as very negative. it_noise will return an effective discrimination **a < 0** and flagged as a mislabel candidate — this is the IRT-based mislabel detector that surfaces likely gold-label errors at high precision. Check the gold answer for it_noise before touching anything else.

---

## The colleague's error

Lumping these as "outliers to trim" conflates two opposite measurement failures. Saturation tells you the suite has aged — the next action is to add harder cases. Negative discrimination tells you the measurement instrument has a defect — the next action is to audit the rubric. Trimming it_noise before you find the defect is the one path that lets a grader or label problem persist quietly into your remaining results.

assertions.text: Distinguishes saturation from contamination as two separate failure modes with different statistical signatures — not just 'both are high pass rate'
Invokes IRT model-fit residuals (outfit/infit statistics or ICC residuals) as the key contamination diagnostic, not just the raw pass rate or difficulty parameter alone
Names the guessing-pattern tell: weak-ability takers passing at rates inconsistent with their global theta (3PL c, unexpected-pass residuals)
States the different consequences: saturated items are non-informative but validity-clean; contaminated items pollute theta estimates and should be audited/removed, not just trimmed
